procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 8 July, 1971 made by the District Magistrate, Jammu cancelling the petitioner's declaration dated 23 April, 1971.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The case originated as Writ Petition No. 270 of 1972 in the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution of India for the enforcement of fundamental rights.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner approached the Supreme Court challenging the validity of the District Magistrate's order, alleging violation of his fundamental rights to carry on occupation, trade, or business. The Supreme Court quashed the District Magistrate's order dated 8 July 1971 cancelling the petitioner's declaration, as well as the subsequent notice dated 9 November 1971 asking the petitioner to show cause why the declaration should not be cancelled.

directions: The order of the District Magistrate dated 8 July 1971 cancelling the petitioner's declaration is quashed.
That notice dated 9 November, 1971 is also quashed.
There will be no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the cancellation of the petitioner's declaration violated their fundamental right to carry on the occupation of an editor and the business of publishing a newspaper.

facts: The petitioner made a declaration to publish a newspaper titled 'Blitzkrieg', which was authenticated by the District Magistrate.
The Magistrate later sought to cancel the declaration on the grounds that the title was the same as or similar to another newspaper, 'Blitz'.
Although the Magistrate issued a notice on July 7, 1971, giving the petitioner one month to show cause, he cancelled the declaration the very next day, on July 8, 1971.
The petitioner was therefore not given an opportunity to be heard before the cancellation.
law: Section 8B of the Press & Registration of Books Act, 1867, governs the cancellation of a declaration.

This section requires that before cancelling a declaration, the Magistrate must give the person concerned a notice, an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action, hold an enquiry, and provide an opportunity to be heard.
The Constitution guarantees the fundamental right to carry on an occupation, trade, or business, which includes the occupation of an editor and the business of publishing a newspaper.
application: The Court found that the Magistrate's cancellation order was illegal because it violated the mandatory procedure laid down in Section 8B of the Act.
By cancelling the declaration on the day after issuing the show-cause notice, the Magistrate denied the petitioner the legally required opportunity to be heard.
The Court also found the Magistrate's reasoning to be flawed on the merits, stating that the titles 'Blitz' and 'Blitzkrieg' are, in fact, different.
Furthermore, the Court rejected the Magistrate's excuse that the title had been "inadvertently cleared," ruling that this is not a valid ground for cancellation under the Act.
The Court reasoned that this illegal act of cancellation directly prevented the petitioner from exercising his profession and business.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the illegal cancellation of the petitioner's declaration directly infringed upon their fundamental right to carry on the occupation of an editor and the business of publishing a newspaper. Therefore, the Court quashed the cancellation order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the cancellation order was passed without giving an adequate opportunity to the petitioner to be heard.

facts: The District Magistrate issued a notice on July 7, 1971, giving the petitioner one month, until August 8, 1971, to show cause why his newspaper's declaration should not be cancelled.
However, the District Magistrate proceeded to cancel the petitioner's declaration the very next day, on July 8, 1971.
law: Section 8B of the Press & Registration of Books Act, 1867, requires that before a declaration is cancelled, the Magistrate must give the person concerned a notice, an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action, and an opportunity to be heard.
application: The court found that the District Magistrate acted with "unseemly haste" by cancelling the declaration before the deadline given to the petitioner to respond had passed.

By issuing the cancellation order on July 8, 1971, just one day after giving the petitioner until August 8, 1971, to respond, the Magistrate failed to provide the legally required opportunity to be heard.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the cancellation order was passed without giving the petitioner an adequate opportunity to be heard, as the Magistrate cancelled the declaration the day after issuing a show-cause notice that provided a one-month response time. This hasty action violated the procedural requirements of the Act, and therefore the order was quashed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the petitioner was barred from approaching the court due to the availability of an alternative remedy of appeal under Section 8C of the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867.

facts: The respondents argued that the petitioner should be barred from approaching the court because an alternative remedy, a right of appeal under Section 8C of the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867, was available.
The petitioner challenged the cancellation of their declaration, alleging it was an illegal act that violated their fundamental rights.
law: The existence of an alternative remedy does not bar a petitioner from approaching the court if a fundamental right has been infringed.
application: The court found that the cancellation of the petitioner's declaration infringed upon their fundamental right to carry on the occupation of an editor and the business of publishing a newspaper.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the petitioner was barred by the availability of an alternative remedy. It held that because the petitioner's fundamental right was infringed by the illegal act of cancellation, they were entitled to approach the court directly.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the cancellation of the petitioner's declaration violated their fundamental right to carry on the occupation of an editor and the business of publishing a newspaper.
appellant_arguments: The cancellation order is violative of the petitioner's fundamental rights to carry on occupation, trade or business.
The petitioner's fundamental right to carry on the occupation of editor of a newspaper as well as the business of publishing a newspaper is infringed by the illegal act.
respondent_arguments: No fundamental right of the petitioner was infringed by the cancellation.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the cancellation order was passed without giving an adequate opportunity to the petitioner to be heard.
appellant_arguments: The order was passed with unseemly haste without giving any opportunity to the petitioner.

Although the District Magistrate's notice dated 7 July, 1971 gave the petitioner one month's time (until 8 August, 1971) to show cause, the District Magistrate cancelled the declaration on 8 July, 1971.
respondent_arguments: The date of 8 August 1971 in the show-cause notice dated 7 July 1971 was a typing error.
The notice containing the error was withdrawn on 8 November 1971, and a fresh notice was served on the petitioner to show cause by 20 November 1971.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the petitioner was barred from approaching the court due to the availability of an alternative remedy of appeal under Section 8C of the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner's fundamental right to carry on the occupation of an editor of a newspaper and the business of publishing a newspaper was infringed by the illegal cancellation order.
respondent_arguments: The petitioner had a right of appeal under section 8C of the Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The illegal cancellation of a newspaper's declaration violates the fundamental right to carry on the occupation of an editor and the business of publishing a newspaper. An order of cancellation is illegal if it is passed without giving the concerned person an opportunity to be heard.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the District Magistrate's cancellation of the petitioner's declaration was wrongful and illegal. The order was passed with unseemly haste and violated the mandatory procedural requirements of Section 8B of the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867, by failing to provide the petitioner with an adequate opportunity to be heard. This illegal act directly infringed upon the petitioner's fundamental right to carry on the occupation of an editor and the business of publishing a newspaper.
legal_tests_applied: Before a magistrate cancels a declaration under s. 8B of the Press and Registration of Books Act 1867, he has to give a notice and opportunity to the person concerned to show cause against the action proposed and hold an enquiry. If he is thereafter satisfied that (a) the newspaper is published in contravention of the provisions of the Act or rules made thereunder, or (b) the newspaper bears a title which is the same as, or similar to, that of any other newspaper published either in the same language or in the same State, or (c) the printer or publisher has ceased to be the printer or publisher of the newspaper mentioned in such declaration, or (d) the declaration was made on false representation or on the concealment of any material fact, the Magistrate may, by order, cancel the declaration.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning upholds the principle of natural justice that an individual must be given an opportunity to be heard before an adverse order is passed against them, particularly when the order affects a fundamental right. The emphasis on the "unseemly haste" of the magistrate's action serves as a check on arbitrary executive power and ensures that statutory procedures designed to protect citizens' rights are strictly followed.
